title: Condo buyer has 48 hours to decide whether a building is financially dangerous
job: Decide whether to waive the condition and commit to the purchase.
trigger: Status certificate package arrives with a short decision deadline.
surfaceComplaint: I have the documents, but I cannot tell whether this building is actually safe to buy into.
believedCause: The documents are just too long.
mechanism: The real task is cross-document inference: reserve adequacy, fee trajectory, planned capital work, litigation, insurance and governance each provide only partial signals.

workflow.friction: High document volume late in the purchase funnel
Relevant facts are distributed across documents
No single number answers the question

actors.incentive: Avoid a bad building without losing a good unit

economics.painCostNote: Infrequent episode, but downside can be five figures in assessments or materially higher carrying costs.

buyer.roiLogic: Tiny relative to purchase value and potential building liabilities.

distribution.acquisition: Only target buyers who already have a package and deadline.

competitors.gap: often not a comparative financial-risk narrative
opportunity to make assumptions and uncertainty explicit

intervention.notBuildYet: No autonomous legal conclusions or universal building score.

experiment.success: 4/10 pay C$399 and 3+ reports surface decision-relevant missed facts
experiment.kill: <2/20 qualified buyers pay C$299, or lawyers say it duplicates standard review

claims.text: Ontario status certificates expose financial and legal information relevant to buyers.
The key product opportunity is cross-document interpretation under deadline, not raw document access.
